segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you not know, brothers and sisters—for I am speaking to people who know the law—that the law rules over a person for as long as that person lives?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he is living; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, while her husband is living, she will be called an adulteress if she comes to belong to another man. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she comes to belong to another man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, my brothers and sisters, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might come to belong to another—to the one who was raised from the dead—in order that we might bear fruit for God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that came through the law were at work in our members, to bear fruit for death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now we have been released from the law, having died to what held us fast, so that we serve as slaves in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have come to know sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting if the law had not said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not covet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from law, sin is dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was once alive apart from law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and I died; and the commandment that was meant to lead to life was found, in my case, to lead to death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Did what is good, then, become death for me? By no means! Rather, it was sin, producing death in me through what is good, so that it might be shown to be sin—so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am made of flesh, sold under sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not understand what I am carrying out. For I do not practice what I want; instead, what I hate is what I do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if what I do is what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, it is no longer I who carry it out, but the sin that lives in me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For the wanting is right at hand for me, but the carrying out of the good is not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not do the good that I want; instead, the evil that I do not want is what I practice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if what I do is what I do not want, it is no longer I who carry it out, but the sin that lives in me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I find this law: when I want to do the good, evil is right at hand for me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I delight in the law of God in my inner person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but I see a different law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What a wretched person I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself with my mind serve the law of God as a slave, but with my flesh the law of sin.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole Roman community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

“Flesh” in Paul often means more than the physical body: it names human existence in its weakness and its bent away from God. Here “when we were in the flesh” describes the former condition of people who are still bodily alive, so it cannot mean simply “when we had bodies.” Some translations paraphrase as “sinful nature”; the traditional word is kept here because Paul’s usage shades between senses.

The verb is the one for a slave’s service, and it picks up the slavery language of the preceding chapter (“enslaved to God”). “Serve” alone loses that connection, which returns in verse 25. Most translations have “serve”; some have “are slaves.”

notes.traditional: newness of spirit / the new way of the Spirit
notes.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so the word could be God’s Spirit or the human spirit as opposed to the “letter” of a written code. Most modern translators and commentators take it as the Holy Spirit, in view of the similar contrast in Romans 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6 and the argument of chapter 8. Older versions often print lowercase “spirit.”

Paul quotes the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21) without its list of objects. The Greek noun and verb are the general words for desire, here in the bad sense of craving what is not one’s own, and the noun and verb match in Greek as “coveting” and “covet” do here. The scope is wider than envy of a neighbor’s property.

notes.phrase: I was once alive apart from law
notes.note: Who the “I” of verses 7–25 is has been debated since antiquity. It has been read as Paul’s own experience, as Adam facing the commandment in Eden, as Israel receiving the law at Sinai, or as a representative human voice. From verse 14 the verbs shift to the present tense, and interpreters are divided over whether that describes a believer’s continuing struggle or life under the law seen from a Christian standpoint. The translation leaves the question open.

The image is of a person sold as a slave and so placed under a master’s power; sin is pictured as the owner. A first-century reader, living in a slave society, would have heard this at once. Some translations spell it out as “sold into slavery under sin.”

notes.traditional: I allow not / I do not understand
notes.note: The verb is the ordinary word for knowing. Most translations take it as “understand”: the speaker is baffled by his own behavior. A minority take it in the sense “acknowledge” or “approve,” which gives “I do not approve of what I do.”

notes.traditional: a law / this law / this principle
notes.note: Paul plays on the word “law” through verses 21–25. Most interpreters take it here to mean a rule or regular pattern, the “law” that evil is always at hand. Others hold that it still refers to the law of Moses: “I find, as regards the law, that when I want to do the good, evil is at hand.” The word “law” is kept so that the wordplay remains visible.

notes.traditional: the body of this death / this body of death
notes.note: The Greek word “this” can go with either “body” or “death,” giving “this body of death” or “the body of this death.” Either way the body is one marked out for death, in which sin has been at work. Translations are divided.

The manuscripts differ here. The reading translated, “Thanks be to God,” is adopted by modern critical editions; many later manuscripts read “I thank God,” which older English versions follow. The sense is little affected.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
Paul’s uses range from the physical body to humanity in opposition to God, and translations vary between “flesh,” “sinful nature” and “human nature”; readers need a consistent choice.
Whether to capitalize when the law of Moses is meant, and how to handle Paul’s wordplay on “law” as principle, needs one rule across Romans and Galatians.
The verb and its cognates (δοῦλος, δουλόω) recur across the New Testament, and “serve” versus “be a slave” changes how the reader hears the metaphor.
This fixed formula recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians and Luke and should sound the same each time; options include “By no means,” “Absolutely not,” “Certainly not” and “May it never be.”
